claim: Spatial attention boosts visuocortical representations at attended locations.
source: This allocation of spatial attention boosts visuocortical representations at attended locations and locally enhances perception.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the study's findings and prior literature, though not directly citing specific data points from this manuscript.

claim: Spatial attention locally enhances perception.
source: This allocation of spatial attention boosts visuocortical representations at attended locations and locally enhances perception.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the abstract.

claim: Spatial attention has often been analogized to a 'spotlight' shining on the item of relevance.
source: Indeed, spatial attention has often been analogized to a 'spotlight' shining on the item of relevance.
evidence: This is a statement about the history of the field, supported by citations elsewhere in the manuscript.

claim: The neural underpinnings of the locus of the attentional spotlight have been relatively well studied.
source: Although the neural underpinnings of the locus of this attentional spotlight have been relatively well studied, less is known about the size of the spotlight: to what extent can the attentional field be broadened and narrowed in accordance with behavioral demands?
evidence: This is a characterization of the state of the literature.

claim: Less is known about the size of the attentional spotlight.
source: Although the neural underpinnings of the locus of this attentional spotlight have been relatively well studied, less is known about the size of the spotlight: to what extent can the attentional field be broadened and narrowed in accordance with behavioral demands?
evidence: This is a characterization of a gap in the literature.

claim: Eight participants (four female, four male) participated in the study.
source: We measured BOLD activity in response to an annulus while participants (four female, four male) used covert visual attention to determine whether more numbers or letters were present in a cued region of the annulus.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design.

claim: The width of the cued area was systematically varied.
source: Importantly, the width of the cued area was systematically varied, calling for different sizes of the attentional spotlight.
evidence: This describes the experimental manipulation.

claim: The deployment of attention was associated with an increase in BOLD activity in corresponding retinotopic regions of visual areas V1–V3.
source: The deployment of attention was associated with an increase in BOLD activity in corresponding retinotopic regions of visual areas V1–V3.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: The cued location could be reliably recovered from visuocortical attentional modulation.
source: By modeling the visuocortical attentional modulation, we could reliably recover the cued location, as well as a broadening of the attentional modulation with wider attentional cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: A broadening of the attentional modulation was observed with wider attentional cues.
source: By modeling the visuocortical attentional modulation, we could reliably recover the cued location, as well as a broadening of the attentional modulation with wider attentional cues.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study.

claim: Covert spatial attention improves behavioral performance at attended locations at the cost of performance at unattended locations.
source: Covert spatial attention improves behavioral performance at attended locations at the cost of performance at unattended locations (Posner, 1980), leading to a common metaphor that spatial selective attention acts as a 'spotlight' or 'zoom lens' (Shaw and Shaw, 1977; Posner, 1980; Eriksen and St. James, 1986; Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Posner, 1980.

claim: Spatial selective attention acts as a 'spotlight' or 'zoom lens'.
source: Covert spatial attention improves behavioral performance at attended locations at the cost of performance at unattended locations (Posner, 1980), leading to a common metaphor that spatial selective attention acts as a 'spotlight' or 'zoom lens' (Shaw and Shaw, 1977; Posner, 1980; Eriksen and St. James, 1986; Carrasco, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The attentional 'spotlight' is characterized by a specific size and location.
source: This attentional 'spotlight' is characterized by a specific size and location and traverses the visual field based on behavioral demands (Eriksen and St. James, 1986; Castiello and Umiltà, 1990), selectively boosting information at the attended location within the visual system while suppressing information elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The attentional spotlight traverses the visual field based on behavioral demands.
source: This attentional 'spotlight' is characterized by a specific size and location and traverses the visual field based on behavioral demands (Eriksen and St. James, 1986; Castiello and Umiltà, 1990), selectively boosting information at the attended location within the visual system while suppressing information elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: The attentional spotlight selectively boosts information at the attended location within the visual system while suppressing information elsewhere.
source: This attentional 'spotlight' is characterized by a specific size and location and traverses the visual field based on behavioral demands (Eriksen and St. James, 1986; Castiello and Umiltà, 1990), selectively boosting information at the attended location within the visual system while suppressing information elsewhere.
evidence: This is supported by citations and general knowledge.

claim: Animal studies have observed multiplicative increases in visuocortical neural responses at attended locations.
source: Animal studies have observed multiplicative increases in visuocortical neural responses at attended locations (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Maunsell, 2015), and human neuroimaging studies have found similar focal modulations of population responses (Kastner et al., 1998; Brefczynski and DeYoe, 1999; McMains and Somers, 2004; Datta and DeYoe, 2009; Sprague and Serences, 2013; Puckett and DeYoe, 2015; Samaha et al., 2016; Shioiri et al., 2016; Bloem and Ling, 2019; Bartsch et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to animal studies.

claim: Human neuroimaging studies have found focal modulations of population responses at attended locations.
source: Animal studies have observed multiplicative increases in visuocortical neural responses at attended locations (McAdams and Maunsell, 1999; Maunsell, 2015), and human neuroimaging studies have found similar focal modulations of population responses (Kastner et al., 1998; Brefczynski and DeYoe, 1999; McMains and Somers, 2004; Datta and DeYoe, 2009; Sprague and Serences, 2013; Puckett and DeYoe, 2015; Samaha et al., 2016; Shioiri et al., 2016; Bloem and Ling, 2019; Bartsch et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to human neuroimaging studies.

claim: Less is known regarding the neural signatures of the size of the attentional field.
source: While neural modulation at the locus of attention has been relatively well studied, less is known regarding the neural signatures of the size of the attentional field (Yeshurun, 2019).
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature supported by a citation.

claim: Spreading attention over a larger region of visual space can decrease behavioral performance.
source: Spreading attention over a larger region of visual space can decrease behavioral performance, but only a handful of studies have interrogated associated effects within visual cortex (Müller et al., 2003; Herrmann et al., 2010; Itthipuripat et al., 2014; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Awh, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Only a handful of studies have interrogated effects of attentional field size within visual cortex.
source: Spreading attention over a larger region of visual space can decrease behavioral performance, but only a handful of studies have interrogated associated effects within visual cortex (Müller et al., 2003; Herrmann et al., 2010; Itthipuripat et al., 2014; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Awh, 2020).
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature with citations.

claim: The spatial distribution of the attentional field is a key feature in the Reynolds and Heeger (2009) model of attention.
source: This is surprising, as the spatial distribution of the attentional field is a key feature in an influential theoretical model of attention (Reynolds and Heeger, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to the Reynolds and Heeger model.

claim: The Reynolds and Heeger model assumes that the size of the attentional field can be adjusted based on task demands.
source: The model assumes that the size of the attentional field can be adjusted based on task demands and that the interaction between attentional field size and stimulus-related factors can predict observed attentional gain effects.
evidence: This describes a feature of the Reynolds and Heeger model.

claim: The interaction between attentional field size and stimulus-related factors can predict observed attentional gain effects according to the Reynolds and Heeger model.
source: The model assumes that the size of the attentional field can be adjusted based on task demands and that the interaction between attentional field size and stimulus-related factors can predict observed attentional gain effects.
evidence: This describes a feature of the Reynolds and Heeger model.

claim: Studies that experimentally manipulated attentional field size found evidence congruent with the Reynolds and Heeger theory.
source: While the studies that have experimentally manipulated the attentional field size found evidence congruent with this prominent theory (Herrmann et al., 2010; Itthipuripat et al., 2014; Kinıklıoğlu and Boyaci, 2022), few studies have directly investigated the spatial extent of the attentional window and its concomitant neural representation.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific studies.

claim: Few studies have directly investigated the spatial extent of the attentional window and its concomitant neural representation.
source: While the studies that have experimentally manipulated the attentional field size found evidence congruent with this prominent theory (Herrmann et al., 2010; Itthipuripat et al., 2014; Kinıklıoğlu and Boyaci, 2022), few studies have directly investigated the spatial extent of the attentional window and its concomitant neural representation.
evidence: This is a characterization of the literature.

claim: One neuroimaging study revealed that the attentional field expanded in the face of greater task-related uncertainty.
source: One neuroimaging study revealed that the attentional field expanded in the face of greater task-related uncertainty (Herrmann et al., 2010), while other studies showed that the responsive area of visual cortex increased in size, coupled with a decrease of the overall population response (Müller et al., 2003; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Awh, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Herrmann et al., 2010.

claim: Studies showed that the responsive area of visual cortex increased in size with attentional field size, coupled with a decrease of the overall population response.
source: One neuroimaging study revealed that the attentional field expanded in the face of greater task-related uncertainty (Herrmann et al., 2010), while other studies showed that the responsive area of visual cortex increased in size, coupled with a decrease of the overall population response (Müller et al., 2003; Feldmann-Wüstefeld and Awh, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations.

claim: Methods for dynamically recovering attentional field location and field size from moment to moment are lacking.
source: While these studies are consistent with the notion that the attentional field size can be detected in visual cortex, methods for dynamically recovering location and field size from moment to moment are lacking.
evidence: This is a characterization of a gap in the literature.

claim: Behavioral performance confirmed that participants could successfully allocate their attention to different-sized swaths of the visual field.
source: Behavioral performance confirmed that participants could successfully allocate their attention to different-sized swaths of the visual field.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's behavioral data.

claim: The deployment of attention was associated with a modulation in cortical activity in the corresponding retinotopic areas of visual cortex.
source: This deployment of attention was associated with a modulation in cortical activity in the corresponding retinotopic areas of visual cortex.
evidence: This is a finding from the study's fMRI data.

claim: The cued location was dynamically recovered from the attentional activity with a high degree of fidelity.
source: By modeling the location and spread of the visuocortical modulation, we dynamically recovered the cued location from the attentional activity with a high degree of fidelity, together with a broadening of the attentional modulation for wider attentional cues.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: A broadening of the attentional modulation was observed for wider attentional cues.
source: By modeling the location and spread of the visuocortical modulation, we dynamically recovered the cued location from the attentional activity with a high degree of fidelity, together with a broadening of the attentional modulation for wider attentional cues.
evidence: This is a finding from the modeling analysis.

claim: The proportion of correct responses was significantly above chance for all width conditions.
source: Task performance indicated that participants used the cue effectively, as the proportion of correct responses was significantly above chance for all width conditions (Figure 1b; t-test, all p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of behavioral data shown in Figure 1b.

claim: The upper bound of the 95% CI for each participant's average gaze eccentricity ranged from 0.29° to 0.64° (mean = 0.48°).
source: The upper bound of the 95% CI for each participant's average gaze eccentricity ranged from 0.29° (degrees of visual angle) to 0.64° (mean = 0.48°; Figure 1c), suggesting that gaze did not exceed the cue annulus at fixation and that participants used covert spatial attention to perform the task.
evidence: This is supported by eye tracking data shown in Figure 1c.

claim: Gaze did not exceed the cue annulus at fixation.
source: The upper bound of the 95% CI for each participant's average gaze eccentricity ranged from 0.29° (degrees of visual angle) to 0.64° (mean = 0.48°; Figure 1c), suggesting that gaze did not exceed the cue annulus at fixation and that participants used covert spatial attention to perform the task.
evidence: This is inferred from the eye tracking data.

claim: Participants used covert spatial attention to perform the task.
source: The upper bound of the 95% CI for each participant's average gaze eccentricity ranged from 0.29° (degrees of visual angle) to 0.64° (mean = 0.48°; Figure 1c), suggesting that gaze did not exceed the cue annulus at fixation and that participants used covert spatial attention to perform the task.
evidence: This is inferred from the eye tracking data showing maintained fixation.

claim: Increasing cue width led to a concomitant broadening of attentional modulation in cortex.
source: The reconstructed visual field maps revealed that increasing cue width led to a concomitant broadening of attentional modulation in cortex (Figure 2a).
evidence: This is shown in the visual field reconstruction maps in Figure 2a.

claim: The broadening effect of attentional modulation was evident in all three early visual regions (V1–V3).
source: While this pattern was evident in all three early visual regions (V1–V3), the effect appeared to strengthen when ascending the visuocortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: The broadening effect of attentional modulation appeared to strengthen when ascending the visuocortical hierarchy.
source: While this pattern was evident in all three early visual regions (V1–V3), the effect appeared to strengthen when ascending the visuocortical hierarchy.
evidence: This is observed in the data shown in Figure 2.

claim: There was a clear attentional modulation centered on 0° polar angle.
source: Much like in the visual field reconstructions, there was a clear attentional modulation centered on 0°, which broadened and shifted downward with cue width – a pattern that was particularly evident in area V3 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in the spatial profiles in Figure 2b.

claim: The attentional modulation broadened and shifted downward with cue width.
source: Much like in the visual field reconstructions, there was a clear attentional modulation centered on 0°, which broadened and shifted downward with cue width – a pattern that was particularly evident in area V3 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in the spatial profiles in Figure 2b.

claim: The pattern of attentional modulation broadening with cue width was particularly evident in area V3.
source: Much like in the visual field reconstructions, there was a clear attentional modulation centered on 0°, which broadened and shifted downward with cue width – a pattern that was particularly evident in area V3 (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is shown in the spatial profiles in Figure 2b.

claim: Model fits explained a substantial proportion of variance in the spatial profiles of BOLD activity.
source: Model fits explained a substantial proportion of variance in the spatial profiles of BOLD activity (V1: for 18° cues, mean [standard deviation] of R2=0.42 [0.03]; for 54° cues, 0.43 [0.03]; for 90° cues, 0.44 [0.03]; for 162° cues, 0.42 [0.03]; V2: for 18° cues, 0.51 [0.05]; for 54° cues, 0.54 [0.05]; for 90° cues, 0.54 [0.04]; for 162° cues, 0.55 [0.04]; V3: for 18° cues, 0.50 [0.03]; for 54° cues, 0.56 [0.04]; for 90° cues, 0.55 [0.03]; for 162° cues, 0.51 [0.02]).
evidence: This is supported by the R2 values from the model fits.

claim: The model reliably captured the location of the attentional field with low angular error and with no systematic directional bias.
source: The model reliably captured the location of the attentional field with low angular error and with no systematic directional bias.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 4 and described in the text.

claim: The group mean absolute angular error in V1 was 41.9° (SEM = 2.86°).
source: The group mean absolute angular error in V1 was 41.9° (SEM = 2.86°), in V2 was 32.2° (2.31°), and in V3 was 24.7° (1.54°).
evidence: This is a direct report of the modeling results.

claim: The group mean absolute angular error in V2 was 32.2° (SEM = 2.31°).
source: The group mean absolute angular error in V1 was 41.9° (SEM = 2.86°), in V2 was 32.2° (2.31°), and in V3 was 24.7° (1.54°).
evidence: This is a direct report of the modeling results.

claim: The group mean absolute angular error in V3 was 24.7° (SEM = 1.54°).
source: The group mean absolute angular error in V1 was 41.9° (SEM = 2.86°), in V2 was 32.2° (2.31°), and in V3 was 24.7° (1.54°).
evidence: This is a direct report of the modeling results.

claim: The absolute angular error did not vary linearly with the width of the cue in V1.
source: Additionally, the absolute angular error did not vary linearly with the width of the cue in V1 or V2 (regression slopes tested against zero at the group level using a t-test; V1: t(7)=0.65, p=0.537; V2: t(7)=1.24, p=0.253; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing reported in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The absolute angular error did not vary linearly with the width of the cue in V2.
source: Additionally, the absolute angular error did not vary linearly with the width of the cue in V1 or V2 (regression slopes tested against zero at the group level using a t-test; V1: t(7)=0.65, p=0.537; V2: t(7)=1.24, p=0.253; Figure 5).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing reported in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: In V3, there was a small but statistically significant increase in absolute angular error associated with greater cue widths.
source: In V3, we observed a small but statistically significant increase in absolute angular error associated with greater cue widths (mean slope = 1.4, t(7)=4.18, p=0.004).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The estimated FWHM increased with greater cue widths in V2.
source: Confirming the broadening of the attentional field observed in the visual field reconstruction maps, we found that the estimated FWHM increased with greater cue widths in V2 and V3 (V2 t(7)=5.63, p<0.001; V3 t(7)=6.49, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The estimated FWHM increased with greater cue widths in V3.
source: Confirming the broadening of the attentional field observed in the visual field reconstruction maps, we found that the estimated FWHM increased with greater cue widths in V2 and V3 (V2 t(7)=5.63, p<0.001; V3 t(7)=6.49, p<0.001).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The effect of cue width on FWHM was not statistically significant in V1.
source: The effect was not statistically significant in V1 (t(7)=1.68, p=0.136).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between gain and cue width in V1.
source: We observed no significant relationship between gain and cue width in V1 and V2 (V1 t(7)=–0.54, p=0.605; V2 t(7)=–2.19, p=0.065), though we did find a significant effect in V3, illustrating that gain decreases with cue width (t(7)=–3.12, p=0.017).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between gain and cue width in V2.
source: We observed no significant relationship between gain and cue width in V1 and V2 (V1 t(7)=–0.54, p=0.605; V2 t(7)=–2.19, p=0.065), though we did find a significant effect in V3, illustrating that gain decreases with cue width (t(7)=–3.12, p=0.017).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: In V3, gain decreases with cue width.
source: We observed no significant relationship between gain and cue width in V1 and V2 (V1 t(7)=–0.54, p=0.605; V2 t(7)=–2.19, p=0.065), though we did find a significant effect in V3, illustrating that gain decreases with cue width (t(7)=–3.12, p=0.017).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The overall gain was greater in V2 and V3 compared to V1.
source: We also found that the overall gain was greater in V2 and V3 compared to V1 (paired t-test, both p≤0.01).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between cue width and baseline offset in V1.
source: No significant relationship was observed between cue width and baseline offset in any of the three brain regions (V1, t(7)=–1.05, p=0.330; V2, t(7)=–2.00, p=0.086; V3, t(7)=–1.61, p=0.152).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between cue width and baseline offset in V2.
source: No significant relationship was observed between cue width and baseline offset in any of the three brain regions (V1, t(7)=–1.05, p=0.330; V2, t(7)=–2.00, p=0.086; V3, t(7)=–1.61, p=0.152).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: No significant relationship was observed between cue width and baseline offset in V3.
source: No significant relationship was observed between cue width and baseline offset in any of the three brain regions (V1, t(7)=–1.05, p=0.330; V2, t(7)=–2.00, p=0.086; V3, t(7)=–1.61, p=0.152).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: A significant effect of cue width on recovered FWHM was found when averaging two or more TRs in V3.
source: When we systematically varied the number of TRs included for each model fit (1, 2, 3, 5, or 10 TRs), we found a significant effect of cue width on recovered FWHM when averaging two or more TRs in V3 (all t(7)≥2.38, all p≤0.049), and 10 TRs in V2 (results as reported in prior section; Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: A significant effect of cue width on recovered FWHM was found when averaging 10 TRs in V2.
source: When we systematically varied the number of TRs included for each model fit (1, 2, 3, 5, or 10 TRs), we found a significant effect of cue width on recovered FWHM when averaging two or more TRs in V3 (all t(7)≥2.38, all p≤0.049), and 10 TRs in V2 (results as reported in prior section; Figure 6a).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6a.

claim: V1 did not reliably show a significant relationship between cue width and FWHM, even when averaging 10 TRs.
source: As described above, V1 did not reliably show a significant relationship between cue width and FWHM, even when averaging 10 TRs.
evidence: This is a summary of the statistical testing results.

claim: Increasing the number of TRs had a small but significant positive effect on FWHM estimates in V2.
source: We found that increasing the number of TRs had a small but significant positive effect on FWHM estimates in V2 and V3 (V2, mean slope = 2.7, t(7)=2.95, p=0.021; V3, mean slope = 1.16, t(7)=3.22, p=0.015), although a significant effect was not observed in V1 (t(7)=1.82, p=0.111).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: Increasing the number of TRs had a small but significant positive effect on FWHM estimates in V3.
source: We found that increasing the number of TRs had a small but significant positive effect on FWHM estimates in V2 and V3 (V2, mean slope = 2.7, t(7)=2.95, p=0.021; V3, mean slope = 1.16, t(7)=3.22, p=0.015), although a significant effect was not observed in V1 (t(7)=1.82, p=0.111).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: A significant effect of number of TRs on FWHM was not observed in V1.
source: We found that increasing the number of TRs had a small but significant positive effect on FWHM estimates in V2 and V3 (V2, mean slope = 2.7, t(7)=2.95, p=0.021; V3, mean slope = 1.16, t(7)=3.22, p=0.015), although a significant effect was not observed in V1 (t(7)=1.82, p=0.111).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: Error magnitude decreased with TRs in all three visual regions.
source: The number of TRs significantly affected the absolute angular error associated with the estimated location of the attentional field (Figure 6b). Error magnitude decreased with TRs in all three visual regions (all t(7)≤–4.48, all p≤0.003), suggesting that more data yielded more accurate estimates, though absolute angular error remained consistently below chance (90°) even when fitting the model to single-TR BOLD responses.
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6b.

claim: More data yielded more accurate estimates of attentional field location.
source: Error magnitude decreased with TRs in all three visual regions (all t(7)≤–4.48, all p≤0.003), suggesting that more data yielded more accurate estimates, though absolute angular error remained consistently below chance (90°) even when fitting the model to single-TR BOLD responses.
evidence: This is inferred from the relationship between number of TRs and error magnitude.

claim: Absolute angular error remained consistently below chance (90°) even when fitting the model to single-TR BOLD responses.
source: Error magnitude decreased with TRs in all three visual regions (all t(7)≤–4.48, all p≤0.003), suggesting that more data yielded more accurate estimates, though absolute angular error remained consistently below chance (90°) even when fitting the model to single-TR BOLD responses.
evidence: This is a direct observation from the data.

claim: Absolute angular error remained stable across width conditions in V1.
source: Absolute angular error remained stable across width conditions in V1 and V2 (V1, t(7)=–0.55, p=0.598; V2, t(7)=1.92, p=0.098), though we found that larger cue width had a small but significant effect associated with larger errors in V3 (mean slope = 0 .02, t(7)=3.28, p=0.014).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: Absolute angular error remained stable across width conditions in V2.
source: Absolute angular error remained stable across width conditions in V1 and V2 (V1, t(7)=–0.55, p=0.598; V2, t(7)=1.92, p=0.098), though we found that larger cue width had a small but significant effect associated with larger errors in V3 (mean slope = 0 .02, t(7)=3.28, p=0.014).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: Larger cue width had a small but significant effect associated with larger errors in V3.
source: Absolute angular error remained stable across width conditions in V1 and V2 (V1, t(7)=–0.55, p=0.598; V2, t(7)=1.92, p=0.098), though we found that larger cue width had a small but significant effect associated with larger errors in V3 (mean slope = 0 .02, t(7)=3.28, p=0.014).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The estimated gain of the attentional modulation showed a dependence on number of TRs, with more TRs associated with lower gain estimates in V1.
source: The estimated gain of the attentional modulation showed a dependence on number of TRs, with more TRs associated with lower gain estimates in V1 and V3 (V1, t(7)=–7.21, p<0.001; V3, t(7)=–9.97, p<0.001), though this was not clearly observed in V2 (t(7)=–1.60, p=0.154).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The estimated gain of the attentional modulation showed a dependence on number of TRs, with more TRs associated with lower gain estimates in V3.
source: The estimated gain of the attentional modulation showed a dependence on number of TRs, with more TRs associated with lower gain estimates in V1 and V3 (V1, t(7)=–7.21, p<0.001; V3, t(7)=–9.97, p<0.001), though this was not clearly observed in V2 (t(7)=–1.60, p=0.154).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: The dependence of gain on number of TRs was not clearly observed in V2.
source: The estimated gain of the attentional modulation showed a dependence on number of TRs, with more TRs associated with lower gain estimates in V1 and V3 (V1, t(7)=–7.21, p<0.001; V3, t(7)=–9.97, p<0.001), though this was not clearly observed in V2 (t(7)=–1.60, p=0.154).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing.

claim: There was no evident dependence of gain on cue width in V1.
source: There was no evident dependence of gain on cue width in V1 and V2 (V1 t(7)=–0.19, p=0.856; V2 t(7)=–2.34, p=0.052), though we did observe a significant relationship in V3 (t(7)=–2.86, p=0.024; Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: There was no evident dependence of gain on cue width in V2.
source: There was no evident dependence of gain on cue width in V1 and V2 (V1 t(7)=–0.19, p=0.856; V2 t(7)=–2.34, p=0.052), though we did observe a significant relationship in V3 (t(7)=–2.86, p=0.024; Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: A significant relationship between gain and cue width was observed in V3.
source: There was no evident dependence of gain on cue width in V1 and V2 (V1 t(7)=–0.19, p=0.856; V2 t(7)=–2.34, p=0.052), though we did observe a significant relationship in V3 (t(7)=–2.86, p=0.024; Figure 6c).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6c.

claim: The baseline offset tended to increase with number of TRs across all three brain regions.
source: The baseline offset tended to increase with number of TRs across all three brain regions (V1, t(7)=8.79, p<0.001; V2, t(7)=6.5, p<0.001; V3, t(7)=5.59, p=0.001; Figure 6d).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing and shown in Figure 6d.

claim: Baseline offset did not show a significant dependence on cue width in V1.

claim: Voxels with a preferred eccentricity outside the bounds of the pRF stimulus were excluded.
source: Within each ROI, pRF modeling results were used to constrain voxel selection used in the main experiment. We excluded voxels with a preferred eccentricity outside the bounds of the pRF stimulus (<0.7° and >9.1°), with a pRF size smaller than 0.01°, or with poor spatial selectivity as indicated by the pRF model fit (R2<10%).
evidence: This describes the voxel selection criteria.

source: Gaze data were collected for all participants using an MR-compatible SR Research EyeLink 1000+ eye tracker sampling at 1 kHz.

claim: Participants maintained fixation throughout the task, with average gaze eccentricity below 0.5° for all participants.
source: Participants maintained fixation throughout the task, with average gaze eccentricity below 0.5° for all participants.
evidence: This is based on the eye tracking data.

claim: Gaze eccentricity did not significantly vary by cued width.
source: Gaze eccentricity did not significantly vary by cued width (pairwise comparison of width conditions using a paired t-test, all p≥0.205 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons) nor location (pairwise comparison, all p≥0.522 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of eye tracking data.

claim: Gaze eccentricity did not significantly vary by cued location.
source: Gaze eccentricity did not significantly vary by cued width (pairwise comparison of width conditions using a paired t-test, all p≥0.205 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons) nor location (pairwise comparison, all p≥0.522 with Bonferroni correction for multiple comparisons).
evidence: This is supported by statistical testing of eye tracking data.

claim: No participant had more than 16 fixations (out of 800–1200 trials) to the annulus during the task.
source: Additionally, we examined the number of fixations to the white noise annulus itself. No participant had more than 16 fixations (out of 800–1200 trials) to the annulus during the task, further suggesting that participants successfully maintained fixation.
evidence: This is based on the eye tracking data.
